paper_title: SphereFlow: Missing Modality Imputation via Geometric Transport on Hypersphere

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Missing modality imputation aims to synthesize unobserved modalities from observed ones. Existing methods treat each modality as living on its own latent manifold, forcing the generator to learn a long, unstructured jump between them. We present SphereFlow, which takes a fundamentally different view: by projecting all modalities into a shared hyperspherical latent space via a frozen self-supervised encoder, cross-modal imputation reduces to short-range geometric transport between nearby points on the sphere. Realizing this idea with flow matching, however, exposes two geometric conflicts: the standard Gaussian noise source is catastrophically mismatched with the unit-norm data manifold, and the linear interpolation path departs the sphere surface into a region where the decoder has no training signal. We resolve both with simple, geometry-aware modifications: replacing the noise source with the observed-modality latent so that the velocity field learns only the cross-modal displacement, and training the decoder with a time-weighted loss that extends its domain to the near-surface region traversed by the flow. We prove that this data-as-source formulation reduces the worst-case off-manifold deviation from a quantity that grows with the latent dimension to a small, dimension-independent bound governed by inter-modality similarity. Experiments on BraTS multi-modal MRI imputation and CT-MRI translation demonstrate state-of-the-art generation fidelity across all settings, while downstream brain tumor segmentation with our imputed data closes roughly eighty percent of the gap to the full-modality oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/WTHH031230/SphereFlow.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Missing modality imputationsynthesizing an unobserved modality from observed onesis critical in medical imaging [Wang et al., 2021], remote sensing, and autonomous driving, where acquiring all modalities is often infeasible [Chartsias et al., 2017, Sharma and Hamarneh, 2019]. Existing approaches treat this as conditional generation problem, leveraging generative adversarial networks [Goodfellow et al., 2014, Isola et al., 2017, Zhu et al., 2017] or diffusion-based generative models [Ho et al., 2020, Song et al., 2020], with designs ranging from modality-specific architectures [Chartsias et al., 2017] and pairwise alignment losses [Zhang et al., 2025] to per-pair 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Figure 1: Two views of cross-modal imputation. (a) Task: given subset of observed modalities, synthesize the missing one. (b) Conventional view: modalities are encoded into disjoint latent manifolds (pixel space or per-modality VAE), so cross-modal generation is long jump between them. (c) Our view: frozen DINOv2 encoder maps every modality to single shared hypersphere d1, on which paired latents (zs, zt) sit close together; imputation becomes short-range transport along the sphere. noise-to-data pipelines [Dar et al., 2019]. As illustrated in Fig. 1(b), all of these methods implicitly assume that each modality lives on its own latent manifold, so that imputation is long, unstructured jump between separated manifolds. Nevertheless, these methods scale poorly with the number of modalities and, more importantly, neglect fundamental principle: different modalities of the same subject share the same semantic content and differ only in appearance. We argue that the bottleneck is representation, not generation. Current methods operate in pixel space or VAE latent spaces [Kingma and Welling, 2013, Rombach et al., 2022], where an MRI and CT scan of the same brain land in unrelated regions because their pixel statistics differ entirelythe model must learn separate appearance-level mapping for every source-target pair. On the stark contrast, if all modalities were instead projected into shared space organized by semantic content (Fig. 1(c)), cross-modal imputation would reduce to transport: short-range displacement between nearby points. This raises concrete question: what properties must such latent space satisfy so that missing modality imputation can be formulated as geometric transport? To answer this, we conduct pilot studies comparing three tokenizersVAE [Kingma and Welling, 2013], MAE [He et al., 2022], and DINOv2 [Caron et al., 2021, Oquab et al., 2023]as cross-modal latent spaces. Two properties emerge as essential: (i) cross-modal compactness relative to subject variabilitydifferent modalities of the same subject should be encoded much closer than different subjects of the same modalityand (ii) geometric regularitylatents should concentrate on manifold with known geometry. VAE latents fail (i): different modalities land far apart, as the encoder captures pixel statistics rather than semantics. MAE satisfies (i) only by collapsing all subjects (regardless of modality) into small region of latent space, sacrificing subject discriminability. DINOv2 uniquely satisfies both: its self-supervised contrastive training [Chen et al., 2020, He et al., 2020] yields features dominated by subject identity with small cross-modal displacement (i), and its LayerNorm constrains representations to hypersphere d1 (ii) [Chang et al., 2026, Kumar and Patel, 2026]. Guided by these findings, we propose SPHEREFLOW, which formulates cross-modal imputation as geometric transport on d1. We adopt DINOv2 as frozen encoder within Representation Autoencoder (RAE) [Zheng et al., 2025], mapping all modalities into the same d1 where crossmodal pairs of the same subject land nearby. Imputation becomes short-range transport on d1: given source-modality point zs, find the target-modality point zt. However, realizing this with flow matching [Lipman et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2022, Esser et al., 2024] exposes two geometric conflicts. First, standard flow matching generates target latent from Gaussian noise ε (0, I)a paradigm designed for unconditional generation from scratch, not for cross-modal translation where semantically meaningful source is already available. On hypersphere this mismatch is severe: ε while z=1, so the interpolant must traverse vast off-manifold void and the model wastes capacity on radial collapse irrelevant to cross-modal 2 Figure 2: Pilot study: tokenizer comparison on BraTS. (a) Cross-modal compactness: 2-D projection of paired T1 (blue) and T1c (red) latents under three tokenizers, with thin lines connecting same-subject pairs; the title reports the ratio dpair/ dcross (lower is better, see 2.1). (b) Geometric regularity: empirical distribution of per-token latent norms z. transformation. Second, even with both endpoints on the sphere, linear interpolation produces intermediates with zτ < 1off-manifold points the decoder has never seen and cannot reconstruct. Riemannian flow matching [Chen and Lipman, 2023, Kumar and Patel, 2026] fixes the path via SLERP but still departs from noise; LV-RAE [Liu et al., 2026] augments the decoder but without geometric structure. No existing method addresses both. We present SPHEREFLOW to address both conflicts. For the first, we replace the Gaussian source with the paired source-modality featurealready on d1so the velocity field learns only the modalityspecific displacement. For the second, we train the decoder to reconstruct from any interpolant zτ with time-dependent weights (1τ ) and τ , extending its domain to the near-surface region the flow traverses. We validate on BraTS [Baid et al., 2021] (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR) and paired CTMRI benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art generation fidelity across all settings. The imputed modalities also improve downstream performancebrain tumor segmentation with our synthesized data approaches the accuracy of training with real complete data. Our contributions: We formulate missing modality imputation as geometric transport on hypersphere, identifying two essential latent space properties through pilot studies and showing that DINOv2based RAE uniquely satisfies both. We identify two geometric conflicts when applying flow matching on d1 and address both: replacing the noise source with the observed modality, and expanding the decoders domain with time-weighted reconstruction. We show that data-as-source reduces off-manifold deviation from Θ( quantity controlled by inter-modality cosine similarity. ) to small bounded We achieve state-of-the-art results on BraTS and CTMRI translation in both generation fidelity and downstream task performance.

sections.title: 2 Pilot Study: What Makes a Good Shared Latent Space?
sections.content: In Section 1, we argued that transport-based imputation requires two latent space properties: crossmodal compactness (paired modalities closer than different subjects) and geometric regularity (concentration on known manifold). We now empirically test these on three representative tokenizers VAE [Kingma and Welling, 2013], MAE [He et al., 2022], and DINOv2 [Oquab et al., 2023]by encoding paired T1/T1c images from BraTS [Baid et al., 2021]  (Fig. 2)  . 2.1 Cross-Modal Compactness Setup. We extract paired T1/T1c latents from 500 BraTS test slices (L2-normalized) and compute two cosine-distance statistics: dcross, the mean distance between modalities of the same slice, and 3 dintra, the mean distance between different slices within the same modality. good transport space needs small ratio dcross/dintra without dintra itself collapsing (which would indicate loss of anatomical discriminability). Findings. As shown in Fig. 2(a), VAE gives dcross/dintra 7.96: modalities land in unrelated regions, confirming that pixel-level encoders force long, unstructured jumps. MAE reduces the ratio to 0.47 but via representational collapseall latents cluster into tiny region, erasing anatomical identity. DINOv2 achieves the lowest ratio (0.41) while preserving well-separated slices: crossmodal displacement is small relative to anatomical variability. Takeaway: only DINOv2 provides cross-modal compactness without sacrificing discriminability, making short-range transport viable. 2.2 Geometric Regularity Setup. We examine the distribution of latent norms for each tokenizer and compute the coefficient of variation CVr = std(z)/E[z]. small CVr indicates concentration on hypersphere, enabling geometric analysis of interpolation paths and decoder domains. Findings. Figure 2(b) shows the results. VAE latents spread broadly across Rd with no manifold structure. MAE latents show moderate radial concentration but lack clean single-radius manifold. DINOv2 latents concentrate sharply at 1 with near-zero CVr, consistent with its output LayerNormconfirming that they lie on hypersphere d1. Takeaway: DINOv2s hyperspherical geometry provides well-characterized manifold for analyzing flow paths, decoder domains, and transport bounds. Summary. Among the three tokenizers, only DINOv2 simultaneously satisfies both properties: cross-modal compactness without collapse and concentration on known manifold d1. We therefore adopt DINOv2 as frozen encoder within Representation Autoencoder (RAE), formulating imputation as short-range transport on the hypersphere. However, applying flow matching on d1 introduces geometric conflicts that we analyze and resolve in Section 3.

We use frozen DINOv2-B/14 [Oquab et al., 2023] with modality-specific ViTG/14 RAE decoders [Zheng et al., 2025]. Stage 1 trains decoders in three steps: single-modality warm-up (Eq. 1), manifold-expansion fine-tuning (Eq. 9), and shared-encoder alignment. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented SPHEREFLOW, which reframes missing modality imputation as short-range transport on shared hypersphere d1, replacing the noise source with the observed-modality latent and expanding the decoder domain to cover the off-manifold region the flow traverses. These ) to two geometry-aware modifications reduce the worst-case off-manifold deviation from Θ( dimension-independent bound 1 cos(α/2), and yield state-of-the-art fidelity on BraTS and CTMRI translation while closing roughly 80% of the segmentation gap to the full-modality oracle.

sections.title: Limitation
sections.content: A current limitation is the reliance on DINOv2 providing cross-modal compactness; modalities without shared visual semantics (e.g., text and imaging) would require domain-adapted encoder or cross-modal pre-training stage. More broadly, the principle of aligning the latent geometry with the task structure should extend to other conditional generation settings where paired source data is available, such as image-guided speech synthesis or satellite multi-spectral fusion.

Single-source (rows 14). This is the hardest regime: three out of four modalities must be hallucinated from single observation. SPHEREFLOW achieves the best PSNR on all four single-source settings, with gains of +0.98 dB (from T1), +1.06 dB (from T2), +1.14 dB (from T1c), and +1.23 dB (from Tf ) over the runner-up Zhang. In rFID the advantage is even more pronounced: the single-source average rFID for SPHEREFLOW is 19.95, versus 29.99 for Zhang (33.5%). This confirms that when only one modality is available, the short transport distance on the hypersphere matters mostthe generator needs to cover three missing directions, and starting from an on-manifold semantic feature rather than noise provides much stronger prior. Notably, the FLAIR-only setting (Tf -only) is the weakest single source for all baselines (e.g., Zhang drops to 32.28 dB PSNR, the lowest among single-source rows), yet SPHEREFLOW still reaches 33.51 dBdemonstrating robustness even when the source modality carries the least contrast-specific information. Two-source (rows 510). With two observed modalities, latent averaging places the source representation closer to every target, and all methods improve. SPHEREFLOW leads in PSNR on all six two-source settings and achieves the best rFID on three of six. On the remaining three, 16 Zhang holds small rFID edge (e.g., 13.83 vs. 19.09 for {T2, T1c}). This patternSPHEREFLOW dominating pixel-level fidelity while occasionally trailing on distributional metrics in multi-source regimesis consistent with Zhangs VAE decoder producing slightly sharper textures when ample source information is available, whereas SPHEREFLOWs DINO-based decoder prioritizes semantic consistency. Three-source (rows 1114). When three modalities are observed, only one must be imputed, and the task becomes substantially easier for all methods. Performance differences narrow: SPHEREFLOW leads on PSNR in three of four settings and ties or slightly trails Zhang on SSIM in two. The average three-source PSNR for SPHEREFLOW is 36.69 dB versus 36.30 dB for Zhang (+0.39 dB), smaller gap than in the single-source regime (+1.10 dB). This diminishing marginal gain is expected: with three sources, even simple averaging produces high-quality latent near the target, so the geometric advantage of on-manifold transport is less decisive. Per-metric observations. PSNR and SSIM are strongly correlated across all settings, and SPHEREFLOW achieves the best average on both (35.88 dB, 0.9530). The SSIM advantage is most visible in single-source regimes where structural preservation matters most. rFID. SPHEREFLOW achieves the best overall average (19.68 vs. 19.98 for Zhang), but the percombination picture is nuanced: SPHEREFLOW dominates in single-source rFID (4/4 best) while Zhang leads in several multi-source settings. We attribute this to the fact that Zhangs per-modality VAE decoder can leverage multiple source cues to sharpen textures, whereas SPHEREFLOWs decoder operates on single averaged latent. Despite this, SPHEREFLOWs average rFID remains the best across all 14 combinations. IS. SPHEREFLOW achieves the highest average IS (2.80), indicating that synthesized images are both diverse and recognizable. The IS advantage is largest in single-source settings, consistent with the PSNR and rFID trends.

Single-source (rows 14). This is the most challenging Analysis by number of available sources. and clinically relevant regime: only one modality is observed, and the segmentation model must 17 operate on three imputed channels. All baselines collapse in at least some single-source settingsfor example, with T1-only input, the best baseline (CodeBrain) reaches only Dice 0.2094, far below clinical utility. SPHEREFLOW dramatically outperforms all baselines in every single-source case: Dice scores of 0.5710 (T1-only), 0.6477 (T2-only), 0.7811 (T1c-only), and 0.6574 (Tf -only). The gap over the runner-up CodeBrain ranges from +0.10 (T1c-only) to +0.36 (T1-only) in Dice, and HD95 improves by 35 (e.g., 169.75 35.75 for T1-only). This result is particularly striking because the segmentation model was never exposed to imputed data during trainingSPHEREFLOWs synthesized modalities are realistic enough to be consumed directly by model trained on real data. Among the four single-source inputs, T1c-only yields the highest Dice (0.7811) for SPHEREFLOW, which is expected: contrast-enhanced T1c highlights the tumor core, providing the richest signal for segmentation. Conversely, T1-only is the hardest (0.5710), as non-contrast T1 lacks tumor-specific signal. Even so, SPHEREFLOW with T1-only surpasses every baselines performance with any single source. Two-source (rows 510). With two observed modalities, segmentation accuracy improves across all methods. The key finding is that SPHEREFLOW remains the best on all six two-source combinations, with particularly large gains when T1c is missing. For example, with {T1, T2} observed (no T1c, no Tf ), baselines plateau around Dice 0.330.38, while SPHEREFLOW reaches 0.6706 (+0.30 over CodeBrain). This indicates that SPHEREFLOW successfully synthesizes the contrast-enhanced features that the segmentation model relies on most. When T1c is available as one of the two sources (rows 5, 6, 9), all methods perform well (Dice > 0.75), and the gap between SPHEREFLOW and baselines narrows. This is consistent with the interpretation that the segmentation models performance is bottlenecked by T1c quality, and when the real T1c is present, imputation quality of other modalities matters less. Three-source (rows 1114). With three modalities observed, only one is imputed, and performance approaches the full-modality oracle for all methods. SPHEREFLOW still leads on 12 out of 14 Dice entries in this regime. The two settings where baselines are competitive are {T2, T1c, Tf } (missing T1) and {T1, T1c, Tf } (missing T2)both cases where the missing modality is relatively redundant given the remaining three. Here, SPHEREFLOW achieves Dice 0.8535 and 0.8533 respectively, within 0.0020.005 of the full oracle (0.8554), effectively solving the imputation problem. Gap to the full-modality oracle. The full oracle (all four real modalities) achieves Dice 0.8554 and HD95 11.41. SPHEREFLOW reaches an average Dice of 0.7473 and HD95 of 19.02closing 79.8% of the Dice gap and 95.2% of the HD95 gap relative to the zero-fill baseline (Dice 0.3185, HD95 169.40). By contrast, the best baseline CodeBrain closes only 51.1% of the Dice gap and 71.5% of the HD95 gap. The advantage is most dramatic in HD95: SPHEREFLOWs average of 19.02 is 2.4 better than the best baseline (46.27 for MMT) and only 1.7 the oracle, indicating that imputed modalities preserve spatial accuracy of tumor boundaries. IoU closely tracks Dice across all settings, with SPHEREFLOW leading Per-metric observations. on 14/14 combinations. The average IoU of 0.6511 is +0.1337 above the best baseline (0.5174 for CodeBrain), 25.8% relative improvement. Sensitivity measures the fraction of true tumor voxels correctly detected. SPHEREFLOW achieves the highest average sensitivity (0.7418), +0.1659 above CodeBrain (0.5759). High sensitivity is clinically criticalmissed tumor regions can lead to under-treatment. The largest sensitivity gains appear in single-source settings (e.g., 0.5651 vs. 0.1764 for T1-only), where baselines catastrophically under-detect tumors. Synthesis quality vs. segmentation performance. An interesting observation is the disconnect between synthesis fidelity and downstream utility for some baselines. Zhang achieves the second-best synthesis metrics (PSNR, rFID) but ranks only sixth in segmentation Dice (0.5080), well below CodeBrain (0.5930) and even MMSyn (0.5546). This suggests that Zhangs VAE-based decoder produces images that look realistic but do not preserve the fine-grained diagnostic features (e.g., tumor boundaries, contrast enhancement patterns) that the segmentation model expects. SPHEREFLOW does not exhibit this disconnect: it leads on both synthesis fidelity and downstream segmentation, confirming that the DINO-based hyperspherical representation preserves semantically meaningful content through the imputation pipeline.

sections.title: F Qualitative Results
sections.content: Figure 6: Qualitative comparison of synthesized images and error maps. Top two rows: T1+T2+Tf T1c on BraTS. Row 1 shows synthesized T1c images; row 2 shows the corresponding per-pixel absolute error (jet colormap, darker blue = lower error). Bottom two rows: MRI CT on SynthRAD2023, with the same layout. Columns correspond to seven baselines, SPHEREFLOW, and the ground truth (GT). Synthesis quality (Figure 6). On BraTS T1+T2+Tf T1c (top), most baselines produce blurry outputs that lose fine anatomical detailMMSyn and MMT wash out cortical sulci, while M2DN introduces intensity artifacts in the ventricles. Zhang and CodeBrain recover overall brain structure but exhibit elevated error in the tumor region, where contrast enhancement is hardest to hallucinate from non-contrast inputs. SPHEREFLOW produces the sharpest reconstruction with the lowest error across both healthy tissue and the tumor. The error map (row 2) confirms this quantitatively: SPHEREFLOWs error is uniformly low (predominantly dark blue), whereas all baselines show concentrated high-error patches (red/orange) around the tumor core and cortical boundaries. On SynthRAD2023 MRI CT (bottom), the cross-domain gap is larger due to fundamentally different imaging physics. Several baselines (MMSyn, M2DN, ModImp) fail to reproduce bone density contrast, producing washed-out or inverted intensities. Zhang generates plausible CT contrast but with visible ring-like artifacts along the skull boundary. SPHEREFLOW best reproduces the characteristic CT bonesoft-tissue contrast, and its error map shows the least residual error, particularly along the skull and internal structures where HU accuracy matters most for radiotherapy planning. Figure 7: Qualitative comparison of downstream segmentation. Setting: T1+T2+Tf T1c on BraTS, then feeding all four modalities (three real + one imputed) to 3D U-Net trained on full-modality data. Row 1: synthesized T1c images. Row 2: segmentation overlays showing whole tumor (WT, yellow), tumor core (TC, blue), and enhancing tumor (ET, red). The rightmost column is the ground truth. Downstream segmentation (Figure 7). The segmentation overlays reveal why synthesis fidelity translates (or fails to translate) into downstream accuracy. Most baselines produce segmentations that capture the rough whole-tumor region (WT, yellow) but catastrophically fail on the finer subregions: MMSyn, MMGAN, and M2DN either miss the tumor core (TC, blue) entirely or fragment it into disconnected patches; MMT and ModImp over-segment WT while under-detecting ET; Zhang produces spatially displaced segmentation with missing ET. CodeBrain achieves reasonable WT boundary but still under-segments TC and ET relative to the ground truth. SPHEREFLOW produces the segmentation closest to the ground truth across all three sub-regions. The WT boundary closely matches the GT contour, TC is correctly localized within the tumor mass, andcriticallythe enhancing tumor (ET, red) is detected with both high sensitivity and correct spatial extent. ET is the hardest sub-region to segment because it depends on contrast enhancement patterns that exist only in T1c; its accurate detection confirms that SPHEREFLOWs imputed T1c faithfully reproduces the contrast enhancement signal that the segmentation model relies on.

sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes]. Justification: The abstract and introduction claim state-of-the-art synthesis fidelity, dimension-independent off-manifold bound, and closing 80% of the segmentation gap to the full-modality oracle. All are validated in Section 4 (Tables 15) and the bound is proved in Appendix A. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes]. Justification: The Conclusion identifies the reliance on DINOv2 cross-modal compactness as the main limitation, noting that modalities without shared visual semantics would require domain-adapted encoder or cross-modal pre-training. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes]. Justification: Proposition 1 states its assumptions (zs, zt d1, angular separation α) and complete three-part proof is provided in Appendix A, covering norm derivation, minimization, and the Gaussian-source comparison. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes]. Justification: Section 4.1 reports the encoder (DINOv2-B/14), decoder architecture (ViTG/14 RAE), DiT variant (DiTDH-XL), training schedule (up to 400 epochs), inference steps (2-step and 4-step Euler), datasets (BraTS, SynthRAD2023), data preprocessing (axial 256256 slices, skull-stripping, per-volume normalization), official splits, loss formulations (Eqs. 16), and all baselines. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes]. Justification: Code and trained checkpoints for both the tokenizer and the flow model are released at https://github.com/WTHH031230/SphereFlow. Both datasets (BraTS 2021, SynthRAD2023) are publicly available from their respective challenge organizers. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes]. Justification: Section 4.1 specifies the datasets, official splits, image resolution, preprocessing, encoder, decoder, DiT backbone, training stages, number of epochs, time sampling strategy (logit-normal), inference ODE steps, and N-to-N averaging strategy. All seven baselines are retrained on the same splits. 7. Experiment statistical significance 21 Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [No]. Justification: Results are reported from single training runs without error bars or confidence intervals. We mitigate this by evaluating on the full official test splits across all 12 (1-to1) and 14 (N-to-N) input combinations, providing comprehensive view of performance variability across settings. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [No]. Justification: The paper reports model architectures and training epochs but does not include GPU type, total wall-clock time, or memory requirements. 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes]. Justification: The work uses publicly available medical imaging benchmarks (BraTS, SynthRAD2023) that have been de-identified and released for research. No new human-subject data is collected. 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes]. Justification: The Conclusion discusses the positive clinical impact (practical deployment with 24 inference steps). potential negative impact is that synthesized medical images could be mistaken for real acquisitions; however, the method is designed for modality imputation in clinical pipelines where the synthesized nature is known. 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A]. Justification: The method is domain-specific medical image imputation model trained on public benchmarks.
